reason: Qualifying stay and some skilled therapy and observation are shown, but personal care and repetitive exercise are non-skilled and the need for each service is unknown.
The hospital records show a stay longer than three days and repeated medication adjustment suggests skilled care, but inpatient status and admission timing are not established.
The appellant contests only liability, and the facts do not show the inpatient admissions were necessary; the QIO notice weakens the no-knowledge claim.
The facts are purely procedural and show no qualifying stay, transfer or skilled need, so coverage is not supported.
The appeal only seeks to waive beneficiary liability for services already found non-covered, and PT plateaued from dementia, undercutting skilled need.
The facts show only setting and dates; homebound status, skilled need and non-duplication are not established, so coverage is unsupported.
The billed dates start after PT and OT were discharged and no skilled care is shown for them.
Insulin adjustments and UTI monitoring show real skilled nursing, but the long period, self-testing and non-skilled reminders mean not all visits are supported.
The stay and condition link are sound and skilled monitoring was documented, but the physician limited the need to about a week and rehospitalization on March 6 ended SNF care.
Skilled therapy after a qualifying stay is supported up to the September 30 discharge, but later coverage is doubtful given unstable vitals.
Skilled PT after the fall is supportable, but goals were met by September 11 and routine exercises could be done by aides.
Teaching safe lift transfers and program setup is covered, while visits to train aides and therapy after the goal is reached are not.
Complications such as urosepsis, abscesses and a fistula support skilled nursing, but routine ostomy care is not skilled.
Coverage is limited to 28 hours a week, or up to 35 on a reasonable-and-necessary finding; hours furnished and eligibility are unknown.
The beneficiary was in a noncertified bed, which bars payment on its face, and limitation of liability conditions are not shown.
The facts are procedural with no clinical information, so IRF necessity for any stay is not shown.
Skilled observation changed treatment in early August, but behavior stabilized by August 12 so later nursing is weak.
Her post-surgical needs fit the IRF population and necessity is individual, but severe pain, the early transfer and missing therapy facts limit support.
